newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Planned Cambodia alliance seen straining govt ties.
newsitem.headline: Planned Cambodia alliance seen straining govt ties.

text.p: Prince Norodom Ranariddh's plan to ally with the political opposition is premature and will further strain ties with his coalition partner in Cambodia's government, analysts and diplomats said.
The prince "won't be able to remain at the same time in the government and the alliance. I don't see how it would work," A European diplomat said at the weekend.

Ranariddh on Thursday confirmed plans to form the Front Uni National (United National Front), and said the opposition Khmer Nation Party (KNP), two smaller groups and Khmer Rouge defectors were ready to join.

First Prime Minister Ranariddh denied the new alliance was aimed against Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP), which he said was welcome to join. Ranariddh expects to form his alliance next month.
FUNCINPEC and CPP, once battlefield foes, formed an uneasy coalition after the 1993 elections with Ranariddh and Hun Sen sharing power as co-premiers.
Their working relationship began to deteriorate last year when the royalists demanded more power and both sides tried to woo thousands of Khmer Rouge defectors.

The CPP is expected to discus Ranarridh's offer at its party congress, now under way. But Hun Sen said on Friday that the CPP could not join the alliance although it would continue working with FUNCINPEC in government and parliament.

Analysts believe Hun Sen could not accept an alliance with his most vocal and bitter critic, KNP leader Sam Rainsy, and that the CPP will soon form its own alliance that would also include former Khmer Rouge.

"We have to be clear that if you are in the government, you must side with the government. When you form an alliance with the opposition party, what does it mean?" CPP Member of Parliament Khieu Kanharith said.

"We're cautious that this might be turned to a one political party system like before 1970," he said, referring to the Sangkum Neastr Riyum mass political organisation of Norodom Sihanouk that ruled Cambodia from 1955-70.

Analysts say Ranariddh wants to bolster FUNCINPEC chances in the next elections, due in 1998, after losing ground to Hun Sen. But forming the alliance more than a year before elections are due would increase friction within the coalition government.
"The timing is not good because it will create more tension between FUNCINPEC and the CPP, which will paralyse the workings of the government," said FUNCINPEC MP Ahmad Yahya.
He suggested early 1998 would be a better time.

An Asian diplomat said Ranariddh appeared to want both to remain a leader in the coalition government and to join forces with Sam Rainsy, the former finance minister who now is the government's most vocal critic.

"The campaign of FUNCINPEC cannot be an anti-government campaign unless he (Ranariddh) withdraws from that government," the diplomat said. "There are (almost) two years to the elections -- he cannot have his cake and eat it."
A European diplomat agreed, saying Ranariddh "won't be able to remain at the same time in the government and the alliance. I don't see how it would work."

He said only the KNP, which is not officially recognised, had formally committed to the alliance, and he was not sure the Democratic National Union Movement of former top Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary and other small parties would join the front.
"I'm afraid that both Ranariddh and Rainsy will become the hostage of the other one," he said, and predicted they would not be able to work together because of personality differences.
